callouts.label: inBloom: a central store families did not trust
callouts.hint: A large gray warehouse at the far top left, its doors boarded over with crossed planks and vines growing up its walls.
callouts.description: inBloom was a nonprofit, publicly launched in 2013 with about $100 million from the Gates Foundation and the Carnegie Corporation, built to hold student data from several states in one shared cloud store. Parents objected that they had not been told and could not control what was held. Louisiana and a Colorado district pulled out in 2013, New York passed a law barring that kind of data sharing in April 2014, and inBloom announced it would shut down that same month (source: S11, S12, S16).
callouts.tip: The lesson is about trust, not technology: a data project fails without families, and their trust depends on clear rules about who owns and controls the data.

callouts.label: FERPA: the school's gate
callouts.hint: An iron gate with a small brass bell on top, at the far side of the second wall, with a teacher holding an apple nearby.
callouts.description: FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, protects the education records held by schools that receive U.S. Department of Education funds. Parents, and students once they turn 18, may inspect the records and ask for corrections, and the school generally needs written consent before it discloses identifying information from them (source: S1, S2). A school must answer a request to inspect within 45 days (source: S4).
callouts.tip: A vendor may pass this gate without parental consent only as a "school official": it does work the school would otherwise do, the school directly controls its use of the records, and it does not re-disclose them (source: S3).

callouts.label: Data minimization (the funnel)
callouts.hint: A wide metal funnel outside the main gate, with many sheets of paper piled in its mouth and a single sheet dropping out of the spout.
callouts.description: Data minimization is collecting only the data needed for a stated purpose and no more. It is the cheapest protection there is, because data that was never collected cannot be leaked. Before adding a field, the school asks what decision the field will inform.
callouts.tip: Ms. Okafor's handout in Chapter 8 promised that Maya's record holds a code, not her name, and no camera, microphone or location data. Most sheets never pass the funnel.

callouts.label: The district ring: governance readiness
callouts.hint: A small red-roofed building with columns in the third ring, and a figure in purple holding a clipboard beside it.
callouts.description: Data governance is the set of policies, roles and processes by which a district manages its data: what is collected, who may use it, how it is protected, how long it is kept and how problems are handled. Governance readiness means having six must-have practices in place before adopting a Level 3 textbook: an accountable person, a data inventory, a retention schedule, vendor contracts on ownership and use, a notice and consent process, and a breach plan.
callouts.tip: This is the school's response to every risk on the poster. A district missing any must-have should stay at Level 2, which needs no student records.

callouts.label: Informed consent (the family's key)
callouts.hint: Two adults standing inside the innermost ring, one in red holding up a large gold key.
callouts.description: The innermost ring belongs to the student and the family. Informed consent is their agreement to data collection given with real understanding: what is collected, why, who sees it, how long it is kept, the risks, and the right to say no. Good consent is specific, in plain language and revocable; a signature on a long form no one reads is not informed consent.
callouts.tip: The key also stands for ownership. Under student-controlled data (Chapter 8), the family can see the record, take a copy and ask for it to be removed.

callouts.label: The trust paradox
callouts.hint: On the grass by the path, a parent holding papers close to his chest faces a school leader in purple who holds out an open hand.
callouts.description: The system needs more data to serve a student well, and families will give more data only if they trust the system, and trust requires that the system holds back. A school that collects too much loses trust, and one that collects too little cannot adapt. The way out is the practices on this poster: collect the minimum, say what you hold, let families see and take their data, delete on schedule and report problems honestly.
callouts.tip: Mr. Chen asked why he should trust the system more than a breached company. Ms. Okafor did not promise a breach could never happen; she promised the district would hold less and be ready.

callouts.label: COPPA: the under-13 gate
callouts.hint: A small, low red gate in the outer wall with a child beside it and a striped height post next to the gate.
callouts.description: COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, protects children under 13 online. An operator of a site or app must give notice and get verifiable parental consent before collecting a child's personal information; the Federal Trade Commission enforces it. The FTC lets a school consent on parents' behalf only when the vendor uses the data for the school's educational purpose and nothing commercial, such as advertising or unrelated profiles (source: S6).
callouts.tip: The FTC amended the COPPA Rule in 2025, and the new rule requires operators to keep a written data retention policy (source: S6, S7). For a 14-year-old, COPPA no longer applies, but FERPA and state law still do.

callouts.label: Vendors and researchers: vendor risk
callouts.hint: Two figures carrying briefcases and a figure in white with a magnifying glass, beside a dark server cabinet in the outermost ring.
callouts.description: The outer ring holds the companies that run the school's tools and the researchers who study them. Vendor risk is the risk that a school's data is harmed through a company it relies on. Most school data lives with vendors, so a school is only as secure as its vendors, and it cannot outsource accountability.
callouts.tip: Before signing: check the vendor's security, limit what data it receives, require breach notice within a short stated time, and state that the school and family own the data and the vendor may use it only to provide the service.

callouts.label: GDPR: the gate for students in the EU
callouts.hint: A gate at the upper right of the outer wall, flying a blue flag with a circle of gold stars.
callouts.description: GDPR, the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, has applied since 25 May 2018 (source: S8). It covers organizations in the EU and, in some cases, organizations outside it that offer services to people in the EU or monitor their behavior there (source: S9). It requires a lawful basis for each use and gives people rights to access, correct, erase and move their data; the top fines reach 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (source: S10).
callouts.tip: A U.S. school usually stands outside this gate, but a vendor serving European students, or a school enrolling a student who lives in the EU, may have to pass through it.

callouts.label: The student's record: student data and identifying data
callouts.hint: A glowing gold folder at the very center of the vault, with papers sticking out and an identity card clipped to its front.
callouts.description: Student data is anything a school or its vendor collects, creates or keeps about a student, from grades and attendance to every answer in a learning tool. Personally identifiable data is the part that can identify the student, directly (a name, an ID number, a photo) or in combination (birth date, ZIP code and gender together). This record is the benefit: a Level 3 textbook uses Maya's detailed learning history to find the fraction idea she is missing.
callouts.tip: The same record is the benefit and the risk. That is why it sits behind four walls, not one.

callouts.label: Behavioral data (the click trail)
callouts.hint: A student in orange holding an open laptop, with a trail of small blue dots and two white cursor arrows drifting toward the folder.
callouts.description: Behavioral data is data about how a student acts while learning rather than what they answer: how long they pause, what they click, which hints they ask for, when they log in. It can reveal far more than anyone intended, such as attention, frustration, a learning difference or a home situation.
callouts.tip: A 2 a.m. login might mean late-night studying or trouble at home. Use such signals to start a teacher's conversation, never to label a student, and do not collect what no decision needs.

callouts.label: The breach crack
callouts.hint: A jagged dark break in the outer wall on the right, with rubble, a gray key on the ground and white sheets blowing away in the wind.
callouts.description: A data breach is an incident in which unauthorized people gain access to protected data. In late December 2024, an attacker used a single stolen login to reach PowerSchool's customer support portal, which did not have multi-factor authentication, and copied student and teacher records from school information systems; PowerSchool told customers in early January 2025 (source: S13, S14). Reported totals ran to tens of millions of students, though the company did not confirm a number.
callouts.tip: Records held in one large store become a single, valuable target. The response: multi-factor authentication on every account that reaches student data, less data held, and a written breach plan.

callouts.label: Retention policy (the shredder)
callouts.hint: A gray machine in the third ring, near the lower gate, with a sheet of paper feeding into its top and thin strips coming out below.
callouts.description: A data retention policy is a written rule for how long each kind of data is kept and when it is deleted. Every extra year of storage is another year of breach risk. A typical policy keeps detailed records while the student is enrolled and deletes or de-identifies them soon after the student leaves.
callouts.tip: Lincoln Middle's draft schedule keeps answer-level records only to the end of the school year, but the mastery summary for a year after the student leaves. The most detailed data is kept the shortest time.

callouts.label: Algorithmic bias auditing (the scale)
callouts.hint: A wooden desk at the lower right with a tilted brass balance scale on it, and a figure with a magnifying glass standing beside it.
callouts.description: A system that adapts to students also makes judgments about them, and algorithmic bias is a systematic, unfair difference in its results for different groups. Auditing tests the outputs across groups: how often each group is recommended, wrongly flagged, or judged accurately. The four-fifths rule flags a group whose selection rate is below 80 percent of the highest group's rate.
callouts.tip: In the chapter's audit, group B's ratio was 0.60, so the system was flagged. A flag starts an investigation; it does not prove unfairness.
